title: What are Terraform modules and workspaces, and how do you structure reusable modules for multiple environments (dev/staging/prod)?
shortTitle: Terraform Modules and Workspaces, and Structuring Reusable Modules for Multiple Environments
topicTitle: What are Terraform modules and workspaces, and how do you structure reusable mod

s1_definition.profdef: A Terraform module is a reusable, parameterized container of resources defined once and instantiated many times with different input variables, which keeps infrastructure code DRY. A workspace is a named instance of a single configuration's state, letting the same configuration hold multiple independent state copies. For multiple environments the robust pattern is reusable modules composed from a thin per-environment root configuration, each environment having its own backend state and its own variable values, rather than relying on workspaces alone to separate production from development.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India a module is the standard blueprint for a branch: you design the counters, vault, and ATMs once, then stamp out a small branch in one town and a large branch in another by just changing the inputs like counter count and vault size. A workspace is like keeping separate inventory ledgers for the same blueprint, so the test branch and the real branch each have their own records. The strongest setup gives each real environment its own blueprint instantiation and its own locked ledger, so a renovation in the test branch can never accidentally touch the main branch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Modules are reusable parameterized infrastructure blueprints, workspaces are named state copies of one configuration, and the safest multi-environment layout composes shared modules from thin per-environment roots with separate state.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Terraform module is a reusable, parameterized container of resources defined once and instantiated many times with different input variables, which keeps infrastructure code DRY. A workspace is a named instance of a single configuration's state, letting the same configuration hold multiple independent state copies. For multiple environments the robust pattern is reusable modules composed from a thin per-environment root configuration, each environment having its own backend state and its own variable values, rather than relying on workspaces alone to separate production from development.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India a module is the standard blueprint for a branch: you design the counters, vault, and ATMs once, then stamp out a small branch in one town and a large branch in another by just changing the inputs like counter count and vault size. A workspace is like keeping separate inventory ledgers for the same blueprint, so the test branch and the real branch each have their own records. The strongest setup gives each real environment its own blueprint instantiation and its own locked ledger, so a renovation in the test branch can never accidentally touch the main branch.

**One line to remember:** Modules are reusable parameterized infrastructure blueprints, workspaces are named state copies of one configuration, and the safest multi-environment layout composes shared modules from thin per-environment roots with separate state.

sections.s2_technical:
A module is simply a directory of Terraform files with input variables, resources, and output values. The root configuration is itself a module, and it calls child modules with a module block that passes inputs. The power is reuse: I write a network module once that creates a VPC, subnets, and routing, then call it from dev with a small CIDR and from production with a large CIDR, so the logic is identical and only the inputs differ. Modules expose outputs so callers can wire one module's results into another, for example passing the VPC module's subnet IDs into an EKS module.

Good module design follows clear rules. Inputs are declared as typed variables with descriptions and sensible defaults where appropriate, outputs expose exactly what callers need, and the module does one coherent job such as networking or a database. Modules are versioned when published to a registry so a caller pins a specific version, which gives reproducible builds. This mirrors writing a well-encapsulated function: clear parameters, a single responsibility, and a clear return.

A workspace is a named state within a single backend for one configuration. Running terraform workspace new dev creates a separate state file keyed by workspace, so the same configuration can manage dev and prod state independently, and you can branch behavior on terraform.workspace. Workspaces are lightweight and good for ephemeral or very similar variants, such as per-developer sandboxes or short-lived feature stacks. However, there are real cautions for production. All workspaces of a configuration share the same backend and the same configuration code, so a change to the configuration affects every workspace, and it is easy to run a command against the wrong workspace and hit production by accident. For that reason many teams, including in regulated banking, do not use workspaces to separate production from lower environments.

The recommended structure for dev, staging, and production is a composition pattern. I keep the reusable logic in a modules directory with modules like network, eks, and database. Then I create a thin root per environment, each with its own backend configuration pointing at a separate state key, its own variable values file, and module blocks that call the shared modules with environment-appropriate inputs. Production might call the eks module with ten nodes and a large instance type while dev calls it with two small nodes, all from the same module code. This gives strong isolation because each environment has its own locked, versioned state and its own blast radius, while the shared modules guarantee the environments stay structurally consistent and do not drift apart. The senior point is that modules deliver reuse and consistency, workspaces deliver lightweight state variants, and for serious multi-environment separation I compose shared modules from per-environment roots with isolated state rather than leaning on workspaces for the prod boundary.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our platform spans dev, staging, and production, and this structure came directly from two problems.

Problem 1 — we used to copy the full EKS and network configuration into three folders, and they drifted, so staging and production ended up with subtly different cluster settings and a bug slipped through that staging could not reproduce. This is exactly what shared modules fix: one module, three callers, no drift.

Problem 2 — someone once ran an apply against the wrong workspace and nearly changed production while intending dev. This is exactly why we moved the production boundary to separate per-environment roots with isolated state instead of relying on workspace selection.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `Module` abstraction that takes inputs and produces resources, an `EnvironmentRoot` that composes the network and EKS modules with per-environment inputs and its own state key, and a `Workspace` concept shown for lightweight variants. We instantiate dev and production from the same module code and run a transfer for Rajesh and Priya on the production cluster to tie it together.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
bank-infra/
├── modules/
│   ├── network/   (main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf)
│   └── eks/       (main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf)
├── envs/
│   ├── dev/       (main.tf, backend.tf, dev.tfvars)
│   ├── staging/   (main.tf, backend.tf, staging.tfvars)
│   └── prod/      (main.tf, backend.tf, prod.tfvars)
└── sim/src/main/java/com/bank/tfmod/
    ├── ModuleDemo.java        (runnable demo + main)
    ├── Account.java
    ├── Module.java            (reusable parameterized unit)
    ├── EnvironmentRoot.java   (composes modules + own state)
    └── BankLogFormatter.java
```

##### 4c. Terraform module and environment root

```hcl
# modules/eks/variables.tf — typed inputs with descriptions
variable "node_count"    { type = number, description = "worker node count" }
variable "instance_type" { type = string, description = "EC2 type for nodes" }
variable "subnet_ids"    { type = list(string) }

# modules/eks/main.tf — the reusable logic (same for all envs)
resource "aws_eks_node_group" "ng" {
  node_group_name = "bank-ng"
  subnet_ids      = var.subnet_ids
  instance_types  = [var.instance_type]
  scaling_config { desired_size = var.node_count, min_size = var.node_count, max_size = var.node_count }
}

# modules/eks/outputs.tf
output "node_group_name" { value = aws_eks_node_group.ng.node_group_name }
```

```hcl
# envs/prod/main.tf — thin root composes shared modules with PROD inputs
module "network" { source = "../../modules/network"  cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" }
module "eks" {
  source        = "../../modules/eks"
  node_count    = 10
  instance_type = "m5.2xlarge"
  subnet_ids    = module.network.subnet_ids   # wire module output -> input
}

# envs/prod/backend.tf — SEPARATE state key per environment (isolation)
terraform { backend "s3" {
  bucket = "nbi-terraform-state", key = "prod/terraform.tfstate",
  dynamodb_table = "nbi-terraform-locks", encrypt = true } }
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the modules + environments simulation
javac -d out sim/src/main/java/com/bank/tfmod/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.tfmod.ModuleDemo

# Real Terraform: apply each environment from its own root with its own state
cd envs/dev     && terraform init && terraform apply -var-file=dev.tfvars
cd ../staging   && terraform init && terraform apply -var-file=staging.tfvars
cd ../prod      && terraform init && terraform apply -var-file=prod.tfvars
# Lightweight variants via workspaces (e.g. per-developer sandboxes):
terraform workspace new feature-x && terraform workspace select feature-x
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: shared network and EKS modules, instantiated by three environment roots with different inputs.

Step 1 — The dev root declares its own state key and calls the network module with a dev CIDR, which outputs two dev subnet IDs. It then calls the EKS module with two t3.medium nodes, wiring the subnet IDs in, and produces a small dev node group. The dev state is isolated under its own key.

Step 2 — The staging root does the same with its own state key, a staging CIDR, and four m5.large nodes, producing a medium node group from the identical module code.

Step 3 — The production root declares its own state key, calls the network module with the production CIDR, and calls the EKS module with ten m5.2xlarge nodes, producing a large production node group. Because all three used the same module code, their structure is guaranteed consistent and cannot drift, while their inputs and state are fully separated.

Step 4 — The wiring of the network module's subnet outputs into the EKS module's inputs shows module composition: one module's results feed another, exactly as in real Terraform.

Step 5 — Because the production cluster was produced correctly from the shared module, a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs on it successfully, connecting the module structure to a working banking operation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Terraform module is a reusable, parameterized container of resources that I define once and instantiate many times with different inputs, which is what keeps infrastructure code from being copy-pasted and drifting. A module declares typed input variables, creates its resources, and exposes outputs, and the root configuration calls child modules and wires one module's outputs into another's inputs, for example feeding a network module's subnet IDs into an EKS module. Good modules do one coherent job, expose clear inputs and outputs, and are versioned when published, exactly like well-encapsulated functions.

A workspace is a named state copy of a single configuration within one backend, so the same configuration can manage several independent state files and I can branch behaviour on the workspace name. Workspaces are lightweight and genuinely useful for ephemeral or very similar variants like per-developer sandboxes or short-lived feature stacks. But I am careful with them for production, because all workspaces share the same backend and the same configuration code, and it is easy to run a command against the wrong workspace and hit production by accident, which is why in regulated banking I do not use workspaces to draw the production boundary.

For separating dev, staging, and production the structure I recommend is composition. I keep the reusable logic in a modules directory with modules like network, eks, and database, and I create a thin root per environment, each with its own backend state key, its own variable values, and module blocks that call the shared modules with environment-appropriate inputs. Production calls the EKS module with ten large nodes while dev calls it with two small nodes, all from the same module code. That gives strong isolation because each environment has its own locked, versioned state and its own blast radius, while the shared modules guarantee the environments stay structurally consistent.

In my project at the National Bank of India this came straight from pain. We used to copy the full configuration into three folders and they drifted, so staging and production diverged and a bug slipped past staging. Moving the logic into shared modules called from three thin roots eliminated the drift because all three environments now come from identical module code. And after someone nearly changed production by applying in the wrong workspace, we made the production boundary a separate root with its own isolated state rather than a workspace selection, so a mistake in a lower environment can never reach production. The result is reuse and consistency from modules, isolation and safety from per-environment roots, and workspaces reserved for the lightweight sandbox cases where they genuinely shine.
